extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and editors covering political and labor beats
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for reporters on covering county/state political conventions, election-day reporting, and labor-union beats — including logistics, story selection, relationship-building, and ethical cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider diverse local constituencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the mind as open as the fields when writing county politics because readers include town, rural, and city folk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember that different sections of a county may respond to candidates for reasons other than party — e.g., local ties, residence in a particular town — so present political stories with awareness of varied local interests and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research candidates' life histories and local ties
rubrics_metrics.description: Look up the life history of each candidate and note local connections (postmaster, residence, etc.) that may explain voting patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use candidate biographies to explain anomalies in voting (such as a county corner switching party preference) and to add explanatory color rather than relying solely on party labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle long convention speeches with running coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominating and seconding speeches are long-winded and delay voting; handling the speeches means a running story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For conventions, provide continuous/running accounts of important speeches rather than trying to summarize them all at once; prepare to serialize or excerpt as needed for timely editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare machinery for accurate convention voting tallies
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting the voting accurately is largely a matter of machinery: obtain complete alphabetical lists of delegates and their districts and check off votes as reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring pre-made delegate lists, mark off votes as each delegate or delegation reports, and stay up to date with the count to avoid errors in tallies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize staff and communications logistics at conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use assistants to take fragments of information and hustle them to a telephone or other communications point held by an aide; the reporter cannot do the whole job alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-arrange a telephone/communications station and designate assistants to transmit speech quotes and vote counts so the chief reporter can remain on the convention floor and coordinate the coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature or risky projections from partial returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Forecasting on incomplete returns is extremely perilous until one is a seasoned analyst; the smaller the number of votes involved, the riskier the projection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not run definitive 'winner' headlines based on partial counts unless the lead is mathematically insurmountable or you have reliable, wide-area trend data; when uncertain, use conservative phrasing noting that not all precincts/counts are in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not influence turnout with news forecasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use stories to inform readers, but not to play upon them so that they neglect voting; bias in the news columns may not be recognized and hence may affect the public strongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forecasts worded so as to discourage supporters of either side from voting; separate advocacy to editorial pages where proselyting is open and evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cautious, acceptable forecasting language
rubrics_metrics.description: When a forecast is risky, phrase it to avoid implying inevitability — e.g., prefer: 'will make a stronger showing' or 'almost certainly will win' with explanation, rather than absolute declarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give analyses showing the basis for expectations (ward-by-ward strengths, margins) and qualify assertions about likely outcomes; provide alternative wording examples (offensive story vs acceptable forecast).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprepare election-day statistical tables and story list
rubrics_metrics.description: Morning papers must prepare both stories and tabulations showing how each precinct voted — tables are prepared in advance with everything complete except filling in figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange a fixed set of tables and story slots (roundup, governor, congressional, municipal, mayoralty, etc.) so incoming figures can be slotted quickly; have bookkeeping/statistical staff and routing systems ready.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slug and label copy meticulously under deadline pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: When many stories come in fragments, label or slug each chunk meticulously so editors don't mistake a 'State' roundup for the 'Gov.' chronicle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign sluglines early, mark fragments 'Proof to [reporter]' and keep clear record of what is already in type to avoid duplication or omission when inserting new paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use messengers for precinct returns and centralized counting staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not waste time at polling booths gathering stats; assign messengers to each precinct to bring or telephone released figures to the office; rely on a counting/statistical staff to fit figures into tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy a corps from bookkeeping and reporting directed by someone experienced in elections; have messengers per precinct and a central counting point to expedite tabulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt election coverage to publication schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: On evening papers fewer returns may be available; focus on the extent of voting and prepare a single roundup or review story rather than multiple precinct-by-precinct accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the number and type of stories to the edition's timing and legal restrictions on early returns; use precedes for occasional early figures and prepare feature/review pieces when full counts are unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build trust with labor sources through presence and routine coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Hang around union halls, linger rather than drop in briefly, and show appreciation for routine news so labor leaders begin to trust and volunteer information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover small routine items (apprentices promoted, personal items) appreciatively to establish credibility; frequent, genuine presence will turn hostile sources into confidants over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat routine labor activity as news (not only conflict)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary day-by-day labor affairs — wage-contract expirations, union elections, membership reports, union-label committees — are often newsworthy though not spectacular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate beat-driven events (contract expiries, scheduled elections), cultivate sources for non-explosive stories, and resist the notion that only violent or conflict-driven items are worth coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor confidentiality promised to sources
rubrics_metrics.description: When a labor leader asks that remarks be regarded as confidential, the reporter should agree and keep confidence; this builds trust and furthers beat reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain and protect off-the-record or confidential information as promised; confidentiality helps secure behind-the-scenes material that informs later reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid propagandizing and maintain factual objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not become a labor propagandist; tell readers what labor is doing using few or no adjectives so readers can decide for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from loaded language and partisan phrasing; present facts and human-interest context without editorializing in news columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit or refuse libelous or overhot union statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Union statements loaded with personal attacks or membership-drive rhetoric may be cut down or refused to avoid libel risk and irrelevant invective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy desks should excise invective and irrelevant campaign copy; reporters should advise sources about legal risks and seek factual, explanatory material rather than wholesale denunciations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beat cynicism and generalizations about union actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume all union leaders are corrupt or agitators because of acquaintance with a few bad actors; recognize diversity of motives and performance within unions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance skepticism with fairness; seek examples of both self-sacrifice and malfeasance and judge individuals on evidence rather than stereotype the whole movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use audience-appropriate items in smaller communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal items and small human-interest labor stories are excellent in smaller towns where readers are likely to know the people involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt story selection and prominence to the scale of the community; what is inside-page filler in a large city can be meaningful front-page or column material in a small town.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain beat continuity to preserve institutional knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter who develops the labor beat and frequent contacts is hard to replace because successors need time to reestablish trust and information flows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, keep a consistent reporter on the beat; recognize that vacations or turnover can disrupt sources' willingness to talk to substitutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipatory beat knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the beat calendar — when contracts expire, when union elections are scheduled — so you can anticipate negotiations and developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan coverage around predictable events and prepare to follow the inevitable negotiations and reports; this enables timely inside-page and feature coverage rather than reactive reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide social and human context to labor reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use feature and semifeature pieces to show the social and sociological value of labor (sickness protections, training, successes) so readers see labor as human and multifaceted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement strike/conflict stories with profiles, success stories, and explanations of union services to give readers fuller understanding beyond 'higher pay and fewer hours.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate fair treatment through transparent coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper should sometimes print even scurrilous denunciations or unfavorable union criticisms to show it does not play down news it finds unpalatable; fairness helps persuade skeptical sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors can build credibility by running fair coverage of unions, even when critical of the publisher, to counter accusations of bias and encourage sources to engage.
